title: SYSK Selects: How Foot Binding Worked
summary: SYSK Selects rerun of the episode on foot binding, a Chinese practice lasting roughly a thousand years (from about the 900s to the 1950s) in which girls' feet were deliberately deformed to be small and pointed. The hosts cover its origin in a story about Emperor Li Yu and a dancer, the binding process (soaking in hot water and animal blood, breaking the toes, bandaging, the risks of gangrene and infection), its status and erotic associations, the social and architectural effects, the late-1800s and early-1900s campaign against it by missionaries, social Darwinists and natural foot societies, and its end under Communist rule. The episode closes with listener mail about Brown Water Coffee.

segments.title: Selects intro and opening banter
segments.summary: Josh introduces the episode as a SYSK Selects pick. The hosts briefly congratulate Kristen Bell and Dax Shepard on their baby, then Josh sets up foot binding as a practice lasting about a thousand years in China.

segments.title: Origins of foot binding
segments.summary: The hosts describe the practice of deforming girls' feet to be small and pointed, and its origin in the court of Emperor Li Yu of the Southern Tang dynasty, who was excited by a dancer with wrapped feet. Other court women copied her, and the practice spread as a status marker among wealthy women.

segments.title: The foot binding process and its results
segments.summary: The hosts explain that binding started around ages four to seven and aimed for a foot about three inches long, with the heel brought toward the ball and the toes folded under. They note that the practice affected roughly half of Chinese women, more in the upper classes, and that bound feet made manual labor harder.

segments.title: Binding procedure, risks and pain
segments.summary: The hosts describe the steps: soaking feet in hot water and animal blood, scraping dead skin, clipping toenails, adding talc, and wrapping with cotton bandages soaked to shrink. They discuss the dangers of infection and gangrene, the need to keep rewrapping, and the pain of undoing the binding.

segments.title: End of footbinding: missionaries, reformers and Communists
segments.summary: The hosts describe the campaign against footbinding, including Western missionaries, social Darwinists, education efforts, natural foot societies whose members pledged not to bind daughters or marry bound-footed partners, and government inspectors. The practice finally ended under Communist rule, when unbound labor became required for food.

segments.title: Social, erotic and architectural effects
segments.summary: The hosts discuss how bound feet were idolized and how women's dependence on men resulted, how buildings were built close together so women could lean on walls, and how China's limited exploration was partly blamed on women's immobility. They also cover the erotic fetish around bound feet, sex manuals, and the women's shoes and wedding slippers.

segments.title: Pride, generational bonds and historical accounts
segments.summary: The hosts note that many surviving women expressed pride in their bound feet and that bonds formed between women during the practice. They discuss a radio interview with surviving women and the cultural norm that made bound feet a point of pride.

segments.title: Search tip and sponsor-style break
segments.summary: Josh points listeners to the HowStuffWorks article on foot binding and transitions to the listener mail segment.

segments.title: Listener mail: Brown Water Coffee
segments.summary: A listener named Kate from Bozeman, Montana writes in praising the show and recommending Brown Water Coffee, a Denver-based company that gives fifty percent of profits to clean water causes. The hosts thank her and remind listeners how to submit charity plugs.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts thank listeners, give social media and website information, and close the episode.
